title: The bird on a thread (Ascent 1.11)
hookLine: a bird tied by a thin thread can't fly any more than one tied by a cord

lines: THE PHONE, THE GRUDGE, THE PRIDE.
cards: Things hardly worth mentioning. The phone, checked again and again. The grudge against one cousin.
The need to be right in the group chat. The show that has to be finished tonight. A little pride in looking busy.
Nobody would call any of it an addiction. Small stuff. Harmless.
Thin little threads, really. John of the Cross has a picture for exactly those small things, and it isn't as gentle as it sounds.

teach.h: A THREAD OR A CORD, NO FLIGHT.
teach.b: First, the bird. In the Ascent of Mount Carmel, John says it makes little difference whether a bird is tied by a thin thread or a thick cord. Either way, it can't fly.
Sure, the thread is easier to break. But until it's broken, the bird is held just as firmly as if it were tied with rope. Second, what counts as a thread.

teach.h: A BOOK, A ROOM, A BIT OF GOSSIP.
teach.b: John is specific, and surprisingly ordinary: being attached to a person, a piece of clothing, a book, a room, a certain kind of food, a bit of gossip, a small pleasure in knowing things.

None of these are sins in themselves. What matters is the voluntary clinging, the grip we choose and keep choosing. He's not talking about the natural wants everyone has, which come and go on their own.
He means the ones we hold on to.

teach.h: A LITTLE FISH HOLDS A SHIP.
teach.b: Third, the little fish. He borrows an old belief about a tiny fish, the remora, said to fasten itself to a great ship and slow it down. Small thing, big ship.
The size of the attachment isn't the point. The holding is. Fourth, why he cares.
John doesn't want us miserable. He says it's a pitiful thing to see people who have given up great things stay held by something small. A favorite cup.
Just one thread. And the image carries its own hope: a thread is far easier to break than a cord.

how: Catholics often use John's bird-on-a-thread image in examinations of conscience and Lenten practices, looking for small voluntary attachments rather than only for large sins.

o: a Latin hymn sung at the close of night prayer
a tiny fish said to cling to a ship and slow it down
a sea monster said to drag whole ships under the waves

games.q: what's inside the picture — tap the pairs.
p: holds the bird as well as a cord
a tiny fish that slows a ship

s: John says small attachments don't matter
a thin thread holds a bird as firmly as a cord, until it's broken.
John means the natural wants everyone has
he means the voluntary clinging we choose and keep choosing.
John's examples include a book, a room and a bit of gossip
ordinary things, not sins in themselves. the grip is the problem.

games.q: you're a bird tied by one thin thread. it's barely there, and you're sure you can fly anyway. what happens?
o: you fly; the thread is too thin to matter.
you can't fly until it's broken.
the thread breaks by itself when you're ready.
games.why: John says the thread holds you as firmly as a cord until you break it. and a thread is easier to break than a cord.

practice: Ask yourself, honestly and without shame, what small thing has a grip on you: not the big obvious ones, but the little one you'd never mention, a habit, a comfort, a grudge, a need to be noticed.
Let it come to mind, and name it quietly, in one word. If you pray, show it to God and ask for help to cut it; if you don't, just picture the thread, and the scissors.

wordCard.voice: Remora. The tiny fish John also pictures, said to fasten itself to a great ship and slow it down, just as a small attachment holds back the soul. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a thread still holds. Until it breaks, a thin one holds like a cord. That's two hundred sixty-five.

sources.ref: Ascent of Mount Carmel, book 1, ch. 11
